chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Serious art survives the business
summary: Wilson and Hinton note symphony halls still sell out and argue something good in music survives commercial pressure.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: But you know, anything different, when the old has sold itself out, they've milked it dry of every penny they can get out of it, anything new that will attract the public's attention to make them spend some more money. But along with that world of parallel is the artistic thing. The artistic people will always live, for some reason.

Ted was at Symphony Hall, the Boston Symphony always sells out, the Pops sells out, the New York Philharmonic, Horowitz still sells out a concert hall. You can't get a seat -- if Arthur Rubenstein hadn't retired, you'd have to get a ticket three or four years in advance to hear him play the piano.

There's something that keeps the artist going, in spite of -- of course, those men have excellent business people, too, handling their careers. But underneath it all, there is something that is basically good that will not be completely snuffed out and destroyed by the business world.
